title: Med-HEAL: Hallucination-Aware In-Context Learning for Medical LLMs
authors: Yiming Liao, Zeno Franco, Jose Eduardo Lizarraga Mazaba
key_findings: Formalizes hallucination detection at the process level within realistic clinical contexts
Hallucination-aware in-context learning reduces critical errors during EHR-grounded reasoning
Reproducible methodology for evaluating RAG-enhanced medical LLM hallucination rates

title: NOHARM: Medical Safety Benchmark and Randomized Study of Physician-AI Teaming
authors: David Wu, Ethan Goh, Adam Rodman, Jonathan H. Chen, et al.
tools_evaluated: 20 LLMs + 4 RAG clinical AI tools (incl. OpenEvidence)
key_findings: Stanford-Harvard ARISE free-choice arm revealed preference: physicians chose OpenEvidence in 22.3% of cases — more than ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and all other external AI combined (19.8%)
24.6% severe harm potential from AI recommendations
Omission errors >80% of severe errors
Clinical AI tools outperformed generalist LLMs
Multi-agent AI teaming improved performance
AI-assisted physicians improved vs conventional resources
Combined human-AI would outperform both if recommendations fully incorporated

title: Generalist LLMs Outperform Clinical Tools on Medical Benchmarks
tools_evaluated: OpenEvidence, UpToDate Expert AI, GPT-5, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.5
key_findings: GPT-5 highest scores across all stages
OpenEvidence/UpToDate showed deficits in completeness, communication, context awareness, safety
Frontier LLMs outperformed specialized clinical tools

title: Expert Evaluation of Clinical AI Tools on Real Point-of-Care Clinical Queries (Real-POCQi)
tools_evaluated: OpenEvidence, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.5
key_findings: OpenEvidence outperformed frontier LLMs on real-world clinical questions
Contradicts June 2026 Nature Medicine paper
149 physicians in specialty-matched comparisons vs 12 in earlier study
Uses real queries from OpenEvidence platform

title: CSEDB: Clinical Safety-Effectiveness Dual-Track Benchmark for Medical LLMs
key_findings: Average LLM performance 57.2% — moderate
Safety 54.7%, effectiveness 62.3%
13.3% performance drop in high-risk scenarios
Medical LLMs outperformed general models by 15.3% overall, 19.8% in safety

title: MedCheck: Beyond the Leaderboard — Rethinking Medical Benchmarks for LLMs
key_findings: Widespread data contamination risks
Disconnect from real clinical practice
Neglect of safety-critical dimensions (robustness, uncertainty)
75% of benchmarks focus on clinical workflow

key_findings: 11 systems compared in largest dental AI benchmark

key_findings: Blinded multicenter comparison in oncology

key_findings: Three major AI tools compared in OB/GYN

key_findings: Assesses OpenEvidence adherence to AAOS guidelines

title: Agentic LLM Systems for Breast Cancer Treatment Recommendations
authors: Vinicius Anjos de Almeida et al.
tools_evaluated: Claude Opus 4.8, single-LLM baselines, tool-augmented systems, multi-agent architectures
key_findings: Best system achieved 0.594 global score - insufficient for unsupervised use
Persistent clinically relevant failures: incorrect recommendations, citation errors, overconfidence
Tool use and agent autonomy had mixed effects

title: CLIR-Bench: Benchmarking Multimodal QA over Irregular Clinical Time Series
authors: Frank Nie, Ethan B. Liu, Yuan Zhu, et al.
scale: 6,600 QA instances, 11 clinical variables, 4 capability dimensions
key_findings: Generalist models struggle with sparse clinical evidence retrieval
Evaluates both answer accuracy and evidence use
First benchmark for irregular clinical time series QA

title: FaithMed: Training LLMs For Faithful Evidence-Based Medical Reasoning
authors: Zhiyun Zhang, Liwen Sun, Xiang Qian, Chenyan Xiong
key_findings: +9% improvement over agentic-search baselines
+15.5% improvement in evidence-based medicine rubric scores
Step-level supervision improves both task success and reasoning faithfulness

title: IMCBench: Multimodal LLM Benchmark for Image-grounded Medical Conversations
tools_evaluated: 8 multimodal frontier models: Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.2, Nova, Llama
scale: Clinical images with synthetic patient profiles, 3 evaluation dimensions
key_findings: Claude Opus 4.6 highest (3.61/5)
Safety degrades for malignant and rare conditions
Accurate clinical description does not guarantee safe patient guidance

title: MedBench v5: Dynamic, Process-Oriented, Hallucination-Aware Benchmark for Clinical Multimodal Models
tools_evaluated: Frontier multimodal models (language, vision-language, agent systems)
key_findings: Strong overall performance does not guarantee process stability
Stressors disrupt contradiction detection and hallucination propagation
Silent hallucination captured through 4 interaction stages

title: PhysAssistBench: Interactive Doctor-Patient-EHR Assistance Benchmark
scale: 1,296 physician-validated turns from real MIMIC-IV cases
key_findings: Current models remain unreliable for interactive clinical assistance
Reliable assistance requires coordination across knowledge, communication, and systems
Key bottleneck: coordination across capabilities, not isolated gains

title: AIPatient Arena: EHR-grounded Evaluation of LLMs in Clinical Consultation Workflows
tools_evaluated: Multiple LLMs across 8 clinical competence dimensions
key_findings: Persistent weaknesses in handling ambiguity (2.57-3.32/5) and diagnostic accuracy (2.63-3.55/5)
Recurrent failures: repetitive questioning, omission of medical history
Final-answer accuracy alone insufficient for clinical readiness evaluation

title: MedFailBench: A Clinician-Built Open-Source Benchmark for Medical AI Safety Boundary Inspection
description: Clinician-built synthetic benchmark and failure atlas that labels medical AI errors by severity (1-5) and safety gate type (6 categories: missed urgent escalation, unsafe remote dosing, unsafe discharge reassurance, evidence fabrication, unsafe protocol execution, source support gap). 44 clinician-reviewed cases with HuggingFace leaderboard.
key_findings: Introduces structured safety gate taxonomy for medical AI failures
44 clinician-reviewed synthetic cases with severity annotations
Open-source (Apache-2.0, CC-BY-4.0) with Zenodo DOI
Model-agnostic framework applicable to any clinical AI system
models_evaluated: Model-agnostic (no specific model rankings in current release)

title: MamaBench: Benchmarking LLM Robustness in Maternal and Child Health Diagnosis through Counterfactual Clinical Perturbation
description: First counterfactual benchmark for maternal and paediatric AI. 434 expert-authored clinical narratives in 217 pairs across 371 pathologies. Introduces Bias Trap Rate (BTR) metric and Evidence-Anchored RAG (EA-RAG) method. Base accuracy overstates robust accuracy by 16-28 percentage points.
key_findings: Base accuracy overstates robust accuracy by 16-28 percentage points in every model
EA-RAG reduces BTR by 5.5pp without degrading base accuracy
Residual 20% BTR confirms counterfactual robustness remains an open challenge
First counterfactual benchmark specifically for maternal/pediatric AI
models_evaluated: 4 frontier LLMs (8 configurations), including Claude Sonnet 4.6

title: MedQADE: LLM Evaluator Limits in Medical AI Benchmarking
description: First standardized open-response clinical benchmark for German. 3,800 items, 10 physicians, 9 LLM evaluators. Shows statistical alignment without clinical caution.
key_findings: LLM evaluators achieve statistical alignment but lack clinical metacognition
Models assign definitive scores in every case vs physicians who abstain on difficult items
Lineage-dependent biases: models preferentially score architectural siblings

title: LLM Jury vs Expert Panels for Medical Diagnosis Scoring
description: Evaluates LLM jury of 3 frontier models scoring 3,333 diagnoses on 300 real-world MIC hospital cases. Validates calibrated multi-model LLM jury as proxy for expert evaluation.
key_findings: Calibrated multi-model LLM jury is trustworthy proxy for expert evaluation
3,333 diagnoses on 300 MIC hospital cases

title: ICU Time-Series CDSS Benchmark with Drift Adaptation and Temporal RAG (MIMIC-IV)
authors: Fatema Ferdous Tamanna, K. M. Merajul Arefin, Md. Abdul Masud
key_findings: Selective adaptation preserved physiological representation and improved vasopressor/septic shock discrimination
Framework correctly identified 26 septic shock cases the retrained baseline missed
PubMed-grounded Temporal RAG preserved retrieval consistency with pre-adaptation source
Drift localized entirely to treatment stream — supports governable clinical AI deployment

title: X-FEMR Clinical Alignment Metric for EHR Foundation Model Explainability
authors: Jie Huang, Pengfei Yin, Zihan Xu, Daniel Capurro, Mike Conway, Ting Dang
key_findings: First token-level explainability framework for EHR foundation models
Novel clinical alignment metric quantifies key-token correspondence with clinically validated features
Surrogate approximates FEMR behavior while preserving temporal dynamics
Supports trustworthy clinical AI evaluation

title: RASC+ Retrieval-Constrained LLM Adjudication — Clinical Value Sets CDSS
scale: RASC benchmark value set authoring tasks
key_findings: Direct zero-shot LLM poorly suited to clinical value set construction
Retrieval-constrained adjudication yields higher-quality value sets with audit trail
Supports CDSS, quality measurement, and EHR phenotyping

title: Quality of Tinnitus Information From Generative AI Systems and Web Search (QAMI)
authors: Hack S, Tessler I, et al.
scale: 30 tinnitus questions, 6 expert raters, QAMI framework
key_findings: OpenEvidence ranked #1 with highest expert-rated quality (4.45/5)
Significant pairwise differences between OpenEvidence and all other systems (r=0.49-0.86)
Completeness was weakest domain across all systems
Inverse relationship: higher expert quality = lower readability (OpenEvidence at postgraduate level)

title: Auditing Evidence Use in Medical LLM Diagnosis
key_findings: Fine-grained behavioral perturbation audit of medical LLM evidence use
High diagnostic accuracy does not guarantee appropriate evidence use
Methodology for detecting clinically inappropriate evidence utilization
Complements endpoint-accuracy benchmarks like NOHARM and HealthBench

title: Bayesian uncertainty estimation improves clinical decision making in medical AI agents
tools_evaluated: Multi-task chest-radiograph classifier + MC Dropout uncertainty
key_findings: Monte Carlo dropout provides reliable confidence measures for medical image AI
Especially valuable in ambiguous or atypical clinical cases
Improves clinical decision safety by surfacing uncertainty
Methodology deployment-ready for clinical AI safety applications

title: ClinHallu: Stage-Wise Hallucinations in Medical MLLM Reasoning
key_findings: Identifies stage-wise hallucinations at specific points in medical MLLM reasoning
More actionable than endpoint accuracy-only hallucination benchmarks
Enables targeted mitigation at specific reasoning stages
Critical for clinical deployment where hallucination anywhere in reasoning chain causes harm

title: Computational Audit of Demographic Encoding in ClinicalBERT
scale: Computational audit of demographic encoding pathways
key_findings: Quantifies demographic associations encoded in ClinicalBERT probability distributions
Maps how demographic bias propagates from training documentation to predictions
Identifies specific encoding pathways affecting fairness
Applies to all clinical decision support tools built on ClinicalBERT

title: SciConBench: AI Agents Synthesizing Scientific Conclusions
tools_evaluated: AI agents + RAG systems across multiple scientific domains
key_findings: Large-scale live benchmark of 9,110 scientific synthesis questions
Tests AI agent retrieval, cross-source reasoning, and conclusion synthesis
Includes high-stakes health-domain questions
Directly applicable to evaluating RAG-based clinical AI like OpenEvidence

title: LLMs Fail in Healthcare: Sensitivity to Prompt Variations
tools_evaluated: Multiple LLMs in clinical QA, diagnosis support, report summarization
scale: Prompt perturbation study across healthcare tasks
key_findings: Quantifies medical LLM sensitivity to subtle prompt perturbations
Lexical and syntactic changes from clinicians produce materially different outputs
Serious safety risk in clinical contexts with free-text queries
Implications for all clinical query-answering tools

title: AI Rater Discrimination Depends on Scoring Protocol in Clinical Decision-Making
tools_evaluated: Multiple AI raters + varying scoring protocols
scale: Factorial evaluation design across clinical decision scenarios
key_findings: Factorial study reveals scoring-protocol-dependent AI rater discrimination
Adult type 2 diabetes clinical decision-making as worked example
Different scoring protocols produce materially different clinical AI quality assessments
Methodological implication for NOHARM, HealthBench, MedQA scoring validity

title: ClinicalMC: Multi-Course Clinical Decision-Making Benchmark
tools_evaluated: Multiple LLMs in multi-course clinical decision-making
key_findings: Introduces ClinicalMC benchmark for multi-course clinical decision-making
Fills evaluation gap (existing benchmarks focus on single-course)
Systematic evaluation of LLM performance in complex multi-course scenarios
Identifies specific failure modes in multi-course clinical reasoning

title: OpenEvidence Accuracy and Repeatability on MedXpertQA Subspecialty Scenarios
authors: Jagarapu J, Babata K, Chamarthi S, Hoyt R
tools_evaluated: OpenEvidence Quick Consult (31% avg), Deep Consult (39.5% avg)
key_findings: OE accuracy: 28-34% across evaluators (avg 31%)
DC accuracy: 38-41% across evaluators (avg 39.5%)
Repeatability: OE 77%, DC 72% evaluator concordance (Cohen's kappa 0.74 and 0.69)
No significant correlation between reference count and accuracy
DC response time ~20x longer than OE (259s vs 13s avg)
Compared to 11 LLMs tested on MedXpertQA: GPT-o1 scored 46%, Qwen2.5-32B scored 14%

title: Arkangel AI, OpenEvidence, ChatGPT, Medisearch: Are They Objectively up to Medical Standards? A Real-Life Assessment of LLM Chatbots in Health Care
authors: Castaño-Villegas N, Villa MC, Barrientos KM, Llano I, Velásquez L, Zea J
abstract: Independent comparative study of four LLM chatbots — OpenEvidence, ChatGPT, Medisearch, and Arkangel AI — on four clinical vignettes (orthopedics, pediatrics, gynecology, psychiatry) with four questions each (diagnosis, clinical management, research, general knowledge); evaluated by external clinicians on 8-criterion Likert scale. Response times also captured.
scale: 4 clinical vignettes × 4 questions = 16 queries per chatbot × 4 chatbots
key_findings: Eight-criterion Likert evaluation (correctness, consensus, bias, standards-of-care adherence, timeliness, patient safety, citation authenticity, contextual appropriateness)
Real-world style clinical vignettes spanning four specialties
Response times captured
Independent (commercial Latin-American) clinical AI vendor initiative — adds geographic diversity beyond US-centric NOHARM/Real-POCQi

title: Large Language Model Hallucinations in Spine Surgery: A Comparative Analysis of Clinician vs Patient-Level Prompts
authors: McLaughlin ND, Srinivas AN, Lowe ZF, Botterbush KS, Patel MS, Avila MJ
abstract: Quantifies fabricated citations ("hallucinations") produced by five LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, OpenEvidence) on common neurosurgical spine topics. Compares clinician-level vs patient-level prompts to test whether physician framing reduces misinformation risk.
tools_evaluated: ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, OpenEvidence
scale: Common neurosurgical spine topics; clinician- vs patient-level prompts
key_findings: Five-LLM head-to-head on spine-surgery citation accuracy
OpenEvidence included in spine comparison
Clinician-level vs patient-level prompt comparison — first such decomposition for spine topics
Quantifies fabricated citations across all five systems

title: Evaluation of Clinically-Focused Artificial Intelligence Chatbots for Answering Drug Information Questions
authors: Ipema H, Munir F, Sarna K, Wasynczuk J, Saiyad Z
abstract: Comparative study of four clinically-focused AI chatbots (OpenEvidence, Clair, GlassHealth, DougallGPT) and one general-purpose chatbot (ChatGPT) on 30 drug-information questions. Three pharmacy faculty scored responses using the validated 25-point CLEAR framework (Completeness, Lack of false info, Evidence, Appropriateness, Relevance).
scale: 30 drug-information questions; 3 pharmacy-faculty raters; CLEAR framework
key_findings: OpenEvidence highest CLEAR score (17.82/25)
ChatGPT second at 15.72/25
All AI chatbots statistically lower than faculty responses
Few "very good" responses from any chatbot — pharmacist expertise remains essential

title: Diagnostic Ambiguity in Appendicitis: Comparing Failure Modes of Large Language Models and Surgeons
authors: Çalışkan YK, Başak F, Erdem O, Kudaş İ
abstract: Six frontier AI systems vs two board-certified general surgeons evaluated 150 standardized ED vignettes (90 appendicitis, 60 mimics enriched for difficult scenarios). GPT-5 95.3% accuracy; GPT-4o 82.0%; specialist consensus 92.7%. Distinct failure modes identified including search-induced hallucinations in web-augmented systems.
tools_evaluated: Six frontier AI systems (incl. GPT-5, GPT-4o) + two board-certified general surgeons
scale: 150 ED vignettes; 6 LLMs vs 2 surgeons; diagnostic accuracy + sensitivity + specificity + triage priority + error taxonomy
key_findings: Six frontier AI systems vs two general surgeons on 150 standardized ED vignettes
GPT-5 accuracy 95.3% exceeds GPT-4o (82.0%) and approaches specialist consensus (92.7%)
Failure modes including search-induced hallucinations in web-augmented systems
Authors caution: vignette studies should not be interpreted as evidence of clinical readiness

title: Machine Learning Classification of Cryopathy Syndromes: A Comprehensive Comparative Study
authors: Nataliya Shakhovska, Valentyna Chopyak, Ivan Izonin, Vira Haievska
abstract: Comparative ML evaluation to classify cryopathy syndromes from laboratory data; 2,686 patient records across 14 diagnostic categories. Identifies practical ML strategy to reduce expert-judgment dependency in a rare-disease domain where lab patterns overlap.
key_findings: Direct clinical-AI decision-support study using ML classification on lab data
Targets rare-disease overlap (cryopathy) where lab patterns are hard to disambiguate
Practical strategy for clinical decision support in rare-disease domain

title: The Reliability Gap in Benchmark Auditing: Distribution Shift and Scale as Failure Modes of Contamination Detection
authors: Wojciech Zarzecki, Jan Dubiński, Sebastian Cygert
abstract: Identifies two understudied failure modes in benchmark contamination detection — distribution shift and scale constraints — that affect validity of LLM clinical AI benchmark scoring (NOHARM, HealthBench, MedQA, USMLE, MedCheck).
key_findings: Two understudied contamination-detection failure modes
Implications for NOHARM/HealthBench/MedQA scoring integrity
Realistic clinical-AI auditing scenarios violate the IID assumption that statistical tools were validated under

title: Consensus-Anchored Multi-Corpus Clinical Chatbot for Long COVID vs OpenEvidence
authors: Yining Wu, Philip DiGiacomo, Ying Ding, William Brode
key_findings: Consensus-anchored RAG chatbot showed comparable mean ratings to OpenEvidence
Numerically higher scores and lower score variability than OpenEvidence
Four-source RAG architecture: consensus guidance, PubMed, clinical trials, living systematic reviews
